task.goal: Create a reusable community-theater scene transition with only light and movement.
hard_constraints: Five performers, a black-box room and one technician; no new set purchase.
Transition must keep aisles clear and take under 40 seconds.
Evaluate audience comprehension, performer load and repeatability at two rehearsals.
task.available_resources: Existing portable lamps and rehearsal notes.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Light handoff between two places
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a change in the location of light to tell the audience that the scene has moved. Before the performance, place two existing portable lamps outside performer routes, aimed at separate areas within the playing space. Keep cables against the room boundary and all aisles clear. The five performers finish the outgoing scene clustered in area A. The technician switches on lamp B; performers turn toward it, then cross directly into their opening positions for the next scene. Once everyone has left A, the technician switches off lamp A. Hold the new arrangement for three seconds before dialogue begins. Budget 25–30 seconds, including the crossing.

The working principle is a visible transfer of attention: the destination becomes legible before the actors arrive. Reuse the same sequence for later transitions, reversing direction as needed. Required resources are two existing independently switchable lamps, safe fixed positions, and a cue sequence recorded in rehearsal notes. No dimmer or blackout is necessary. This assumes the lamps create distinguishable areas under the room’s ambient light and one technician can operate both from a safe position. It communicates a change of place more reliably than the identity of that place; the next scene’s opening arrangement must supply that detail.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: At rehearsal one, show this transition and a comparator using the same crossing under steady light to a few observers unfamiliar with the staging. Ask where their attention went and whether the scene changed location. Time both versions and ask each performer to rate effort and cue uncertainty. At rehearsal two, repeat the chosen sequence three times after running the preceding scene. Record duration, missed cues, route conflicts and comprehension in rehearsal notes. Reject or simplify it if the lighting adds no clarity, any run reaches 40 seconds, or operation requires the technician to enter an aisle.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The ensemble redraws the room
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep the light steady and transform the performers’ spatial relationships into the architecture of the next scene. For example, five performers end as a tight inward-facing group; over three counted phrases they open into two opposing pairs and a fifth person between them, establishing a hearing, confrontation or formal meeting. Each performer takes a short direct route entirely inside the playing area. They stop together, orient their gaze toward the new focal person and hold for three seconds. Budget 20–25 seconds.

The mechanism is a change in social geometry: proximity, facing and status make the new situation visible without moving scenery. For reuse, give each recurring location one distinctive opening formation and write the five routes in rehearsal notes. Adapt formations to the actual script rather than adding unexplained symbolic gestures. An existing lamp can provide steady illumination; the technician maintains the state and watches for unsafe visibility.

This needs enough internal floor space for five short routes and performers who can sustain clear, comfortable positions. It requires no lamp switching, furniture, props or purchases. Its limit is specificity: bodies can establish a relationship or type of space, but may not distinguish two otherwise similar rooms. Avoid making performers hold strenuous poses as imaginary scenery. The outcome depends on a readable difference between the outgoing and incoming formations.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: At rehearsal one, compare the designed transformation with an ordinary walk to the same opening positions, using identical lighting and no dialogue. Ask unfamiliar observers to describe the resulting relationships and whether they recognized a new scene. Collect performer effort ratings and identify difficult crossings. At rehearsal two, run the transformation three times from the preceding scene, checking duration, position accuracy and synchronized arrival. Keep it only if observers understand the intended relationship at least as well as with the comparator and the formation remains comfortable and repeatable below 40 seconds.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A movement phrase marks a jump in time
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a repeated action with a changed ending to signal that time has passed. Choose one short, script-relevant movement available to all five performers, such as turning toward an imagined doorway. At the outgoing scene’s end, everyone performs it once at ordinary speed, resets in place, then repeats it slowly. During the slow repetition they change posture and facing into the next scene’s opening state. Hold that final image for three seconds before speech. Keep the complete sequence to 18–25 seconds, with no travel outside the playing area.

The mechanism is repetition followed by visible difference: the audience sees an earlier moment recur and resolve into a later condition. Establish the convention at its first use, then retain the same phrase and rhythm for later time jumps. An existing portable lamp provides steady light, leaving the technician one stable state to maintain. Record the phrase, counts and final positions in rehearsal notes.

This assumes the script contains a meaningful before-and-after contrast that the performers can show physically. Small changes in energy, gaze or stance should express character circumstances rather than rely on age stereotypes. It works best for elapsed time, memory or recurring routines; it may confuse audiences if used indiscriminately for changes of location. Its principal uncertainty is whether repetition reads as a transition or as action continuing within the same scene. No new equipment, sound or set is required.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: At rehearsal one, show unfamiliar observers the repeated phrase and a comparator consisting of a simple pause followed by the same new posture. Ask whether time passed, whether the scene changed and what physical difference they noticed. Ask performers about counting difficulty and physical effort. At rehearsal two, repeat the transition three times after the outgoing scene and record duration, synchronization errors and effort. Reject the device if observers consistently interpret it as continuous action, or if the repetition adds performer load without improving comprehension. Every run must stay below 40 seconds with aisles clear.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A dark interval closes the scene
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a brief interruption of visibility as a reusable boundary between scenes. The five performers freeze at the outgoing scene’s final moment. The technician switches off the existing performance lamps for two seconds while everyone remains still, then restores the same lighting. Under restored light, performers release character posture and walk directly to their next opening positions within the playing area. They settle, take one shared breath and begin the next scene. Budget 15–25 seconds, including the dark interval and reset.

The mechanism is visual punctuation: briefly removing the stage image closes the preceding scene, allowing the subsequent movement to read as a reset. Unlike a transfer between illuminated locations, this convention can mark a scene boundary even when both scenes occupy the same space. It does not by itself explain a new location or how much time has passed; the next scene must establish those details.

Use only existing lamps, fixed safely outside walking routes, with cables secured away from aisles. Record the freeze, lighting cues and five short routes in rehearsal notes. One technician must be able to switch the relevant lamps safely from a single position. Keep required exit and aisle illumination operating throughout. No performer moves during the dark interval, and travel begins only when visibility returns.

This assumes the existing lamps permit a clearly perceptible interruption without interfering with safety lighting. If ambient light makes the interruption barely noticeable, or the lamps cannot be controlled together, this mechanism may not be practical.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
At rehearsal one, show a few unfamiliar observers the outgoing scene ending and incoming opening, first with a lit pause and then with the dark interval; reverse the order for some observers if feasible. Keep routes and timing otherwise identical. Ask whether they perceived a scene boundary and whether the reset looked intentional. Collect performer effort and cue-confidence ratings, and note technician workload.

At rehearsal two, repeat both versions after the preceding scene. Time three runs of the proposed transition and record missed freezes, premature movement, route conflicts and observer interpretations. Reject the dark interval if it adds confusion or offers no clearer boundary than the lit pause. Require every run to finish below 40 seconds, aisles to remain clear, and performers to report manageable effort and reliable cues at both rehearsals.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A shadow landmark establishes the next place
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use enlarged shadows as temporary scenery. For a transition into a passage or enclosed meeting place, two performers stand apart near a fixed portable lamp so their shadows form tall sides of an opening on an existing plain wall. They keep their arms comfortably lowered; the gap between their shadows supplies the doorway. The other three performers approach that opening within the playing area and settle into the next scene’s opening positions. Hold the image for three seconds, then let the two shadow makers step away from the beam and join the scene. Target 20–30 seconds.

The mechanism is optical enlargement: ordinary bodies briefly become an architectural landmark, giving the incoming action a visible destination without scenery. Unlike a formation that communicates social relationships, the projected image supplies a spatial feature. Reuse the doorway for recurring entrances or enclosed locations, retaining its proportions and approach direction.

This requires an existing lamp that produces reasonably distinct shadows, a suitable wall, and enough space to keep performers safely away from the lamp. Fix the lamp outside all routes, keep cables and performers clear of aisles, and preserve required safety lighting. One technician switches it on at the outgoing scene’s final stillness and off after the arrival image; existing general illumination must remain sufficient for movement. Record lamp position, performer positions and cues in rehearsal notes. No purchases, props, sound or strenuous holds are needed.

The main uncertainty is whether available lamps and ambient light produce a recognizable opening. This mechanism suits scripts with a meaningful threshold; it cannot reliably identify a particular building. Reject it if achieving a readable shadow requires unsafe proximity, obstructing an aisle or an uncomfortable stance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
At rehearsal one, first inspect shadow clarity from the actual audience positions. Then show a few unfamiliar observers the transition and a simple comparator: the same arrivals under steady light without the shadow doorway. Ask what spatial feature they perceived and whether the arrival established a new place. Record duration, each performer’s effort and cue uncertainty, and technician difficulty.

At rehearsal two, repeat both versions after the preceding scene, including three timed runs of the shadow version. Again collect audience interpretations and performer effort ratings; record missed positions, inconsistent shadows and cue errors. Keep the device only if the doorway improves spatial comprehension, the workload remains manageable, and all three runs reproduce the image with clear aisles in under 40 seconds.

EXPAND.title: A dark interval makes a clean cut
EXPAND.proposal:
Use a brief loss of the visible image to separate scenes, without requiring a visible journey between locations. All five performers finish in positions from which they can reach their next opening stance with planted feet: turning, changing gaze or relaxing into a different posture. The technician switches off the existing portable lamps for two seconds, then restores the same lighting. The changed tableau holds for three seconds before dialogue. Target duration: 8–12 seconds.

The mechanism is interruption of visual continuity. Darkness supplies the scene boundary; the performers do not need to enact relocation. Unlike the prior light-handoff route, this requires neither a second illuminated destination nor a crossing between areas. It suits transitions where the next scene can start on substantially the same footprint.

Before use, the technician checks whether existing controls can extinguish and restore the performance lamps safely from one operating position. Leave emergency and aisle lighting untouched. Keep lamps and cables outside all routes. Record the cue, two-second interval and five destination stances in rehearsal notes. No performer travels while the playing space is dark. If the lamps restart slowly, ambient light prevents a useful interruption, or the script requires substantial repositioning, do not use this mechanism.

The audience may understand a scene break without knowing the new place or elapsed time. Those details must become apparent through the next scene. If a cue fails, performers remain still and the technician restores the starting light; rehearse that recovery within the 40-second ceiling.
EXPAND.experiment: At rehearsal one, the technician owns a bounded trial comparing the dark cut with the prior two-area light handoff for the same scene pair. Use a few observers unfamiliar with the staging; ask whether a new scene began and where and when they think it occurs. Record duration, performer cue uncertainty and technician workload. At rehearsal two, repeat each version three times from the preceding scene. Stop a run immediately for unsafe visibility or unintended travel. Reject the dark cut if any run reaches 40 seconds, comprehension is worse, or its reduced walking merely shifts difficulty into unreliable lamp operation.

EXPAND.title: Carry one action across the scene boundary
EXPAND.proposal:
Give the outgoing scene’s final action to one performer and its completion to another performer in the incoming scene. For example, performer A extends an empty hand toward someone; performer B, already elsewhere in the playing area, completes the receiving motion as a different character in the next scene. Nothing is passed. A becomes still as B begins. The other three performers turn or take one short, predetermined step into their new roles. Hold the completed action briefly, then begin the next dialogue. Target duration: 10–18 seconds under steady illumination from existing lamps.

The mechanism is continuity of an unfinished action across a discontinuity in story. A clear initiation and completion connect the two scenes while the change of actor and dramatic context makes the cut visible. This differs from repeating a movement to suggest elapsed time: perform the action only once, divided between two people, with no reset or slow replay.

Choose a scene pair whose script supports a meaningful visual connection, such as offering and accepting, looking and being seen, or reaching and withdrawing. Write the exact initiation, takeover point and ending in rehearsal notes. All five performers remain inside the playing area, with lamps and cables fixed away from aisles. The technician maintains one light state.

This requires readable sightlines and an action that makes sense without a physical prop. Avoid precision catches, contact or balancing. If B misses the takeover, A settles the gesture and everyone proceeds directly to the opening tableau. Do not add another attempt. The principal risk is that observers interpret the gesture as an interaction within one continuous scene.
EXPAND.experiment: At rehearsal one, the director owns a trial of one scene pair, comparing the divided action with the prior ordinary transformation into the same opening formation. Ask unfamiliar observers whether the scene changed, who acted on whom and whether an object seemed missing. Collect effort and coordination ratings from all five performers. At rehearsal two, run both versions three times after the preceding scene, including one deliberately delayed takeover to inspect recovery. Stop for route conflict; reject if any run reaches 40 seconds, observers consistently infer continuous action, or added coordination produces no clearer or more useful transition than the simple formation change.

EXPAND.title: Let shadows become the next dramatic space
EXPAND.proposal:
Transform a scene played by visible bodies into a scene played through their shadows. Use one existing portable lamp in a fixed, stable position aimed toward a clear wall inside the playing area. Begin with general illumination from the other available lamps. At the outgoing scene’s end, the five performers turn toward the wall and take short, assigned steps to positions between the fixed lamp and wall. The technician switches off the general lamps, leaving the shadow lamp on. Performers settle into the next scene’s opening shadow image and hold for three seconds. Target duration: 20–30 seconds.

The mechanism is a change of representational medium: the audience moves from watching people directly to reading their projected silhouettes. Shadow size and separation can establish a dream, recollection or threatening imagined space without scenery. Unlike the prior transfer between illuminated locations, the destination is an image made by the performers, rather than another pool of light they occupy.

This is conditional on an existing lamp producing sufficiently crisp shadows, a usable wall and audience sightlines that make the image visible. The technician owns a preliminary optical check before choreography begins. Use only lamps that operate safely in their normal position; do not remove shades, cover bulbs or improvise mounts. Keep performers clear of hot equipment and fix cables against the boundary. Record five positions and short routes in rehearsal notes.

The route is unsuitable if ambient light washes out silhouettes or the wall cannot accommodate five readable figures. Avoid overlapping bodies unless the combined image is intentional. If the shadow state fails, restore general light and continue in the same opening positions. The next scene must remain playable in that fallback state.
EXPAND.experiment: At rehearsal one, compare a ten-second shadow prototype with the prior light handoff, using the same intended shift into a remembered or imagined scene. The technician stops development immediately if safe existing equipment cannot produce readable silhouettes. Ask observers what changed in the story’s reality or perspective, and ask performers about orientation, effort and dependence on exact placement. At rehearsal two, repeat both transitions three times and inspect from different audience seats. Reject the shadow route if any run reaches 40 seconds, aisles or equipment clearances are compromised, or its interpretation is no clearer than the handoff after accounting for extra positioning work and restricted sightlines.

EXPAND.title: Redraw the room with a recoverable arrival
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “The ensemble redraws the room.” Preserve steady light, five short routes inside the playing area, a distinctive opening formation and a three-second hold. Add a procedure for interrupted arrivals: nominate one of the five performers as movement captain. Everyone moves during an eight-count phrase, then stops on a clear internal beat. If a route is obstructed, that performer stops safely instead of catching up; the others do not retrace their steps. The captain starts the next scene after the hold, accepting a rehearsed, approximate formation. Target 20–25 seconds, including recovery.

The mechanism remains social geometry: facing, distance and attention establish the incoming situation. The changed action prevents one late arrival from triggering extra crossings or an indefinite wait. Before adopting it, the performers must demonstrate that the next scene can begin from both the intended formation and safe nearby positions. If exact placement is essential, shorten the routes or use a planted-foot change of facing instead.

Use existing lamps and record routes, counts and acceptable fallback positions in rehearsal notes. Keep lamps, cables and all movement outside aisles. This should reduce coordination burden after interruptions, but accepting approximate positions may weaken the image. It still communicates relationships more readily than a specific address or date.
EXPAND.experiment: At rehearsal one, the five performers prototype one scene pair; the movement captain leads the trial. Compare the original exact-arrival version with the revised procedure, including one deliberately late arrival. Ask unfamiliar observers whether a new scene began and what relationships they understood. Record duration and each performer's effort and cue uncertainty. Stop for route conflict or any attempt to recover by rushing. At rehearsal two, run the revised transition three times after the preceding scene, once with a delayed mover. Record comprehension, duration, formation readability and recovery consistency. Keep it only if every run stays below 40 seconds, aisles remain clear, and the approximate formation supports the next scene without materially reducing comprehension.

EXPAND.title: Accept the destination light before anyone crosses
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade of “Light handoff between two places.” Preserve two fixed lamps illuminating separate playing areas, destination light before movement, direct crossings, outgoing light off after departure and a three-second opening hold. Change the handoff: the technician switches on destination B while everyone remains in A. A nominated performer checks that B visibly illuminates the landing area and route, then initiates the crossing with a head turn. Until that acceptance, all five remain in A.

Allow one three-second acceptance window. If B fails or visibility is doubtful, the nominated performer turns the group inward instead; everyone establishes a rehearsed version of the next scene within A under its existing light. The technician leaves A on and makes no further repair attempt during the transition. If B fails during a crossing, keep A on, stop travel and begin from safe visible positions. Rehearse this fallback before use. Target 25–30 seconds, with a 35-second rehearsal ceiling that leaves margin below 40.

The primary mechanism remains a visible transfer of attention between locations. The addition closes the gap between a lighting command and usable illumination. It costs a brief acceptance pause and requires the incoming scene to tolerate an alternate footprint. Two independently controllable existing lamps, safe cable placement, readable ambient conditions and one operating position are prerequisites. If the fallback cannot be played safely, use the steady-light formation change for that scene pair instead.
EXPAND.experiment: The technician and nominated performer own the first rehearsal trial. Compare the original handoff with the accepted-light version for the same scene pair; include one destination lamp deliberately left off. Ask unfamiliar observers whether the scene changed and where their attention went. Collect all five performers' effort and cue-confidence ratings and the technician's workload assessment. Stop immediately for uncertain footing or aisle use. At rehearsal two, run three transitions from the preceding scene: normal, destination unavailable, and a safely simulated interruption before crossing begins. Record comprehension, duration, missed acceptance cues and fallback consistency. Retain only if all runs finish within 35 seconds and the added pause yields a reliable decision without making the transition confusing.

EXPAND.title: An open-view neutral interval closes one scene
EXPAND.proposal:
Create a reusable punctuation convention without relocating the ensemble or interrupting illumination. At the outgoing scene's final beat, all five performers release character-specific posture, lower their gaze and stand comfortably with arms resting naturally. Hold this neutral state for four seconds. A nominated performer then lifts their gaze into the next character's focus; the others follow within two beats and begin the next scene. Use existing steady lamps. Target 10–15 seconds, entirely on the existing footprint.

The mechanism is a visible withdrawal and restoration of dramatic engagement: the performers briefly stop presenting a fictional situation. Unlike a formation change, it does not depend on new spatial relationships; unlike a repeated action, it does not enact elapsed time. It removes the assumption that a scene boundary needs darkness, travel or a visual link between scenes.

Record the neutral posture, duration and initiating performer in rehearsal notes. All five must be able to enter the next scene from their current positions; if necessary, make only comfortable planted-foot turns when character engagement returns. The technician maintains illumination and keeps lamps and cables outside aisles. If someone misses the neutral interval, they join it without restarting. If the initiating cue is missed, everyone resumes on a rehearsed final count, keeping the whole sequence below 20 seconds.

Compared with an ordinary pause, the explicit release may make the boundary clearer, but it may also look like dropped concentration. It requires a production style that accepts visible performers between scenes. It cannot by itself identify the new place or time; the incoming scene must supply that information.
EXPAND.experiment: At rehearsal one, the nominated performer leads a prototype against an ordinary pause of equal length, using the same scene pair and steady light. Ask unfamiliar observers whether the scene ended, whether the neutral interval looked intentional and when the new scene began. Collect effort and counting-load ratings from all five performers. Stop development if observers predominantly read the release as an acting mistake or if the next scene requires unsafe repositioning. At rehearsal two, repeat three times after the preceding scene, including one missed initiating cue. Record duration, audience comprehension, performer load and consistency of the count-based recovery. Adopt only if all runs remain below 40 seconds with clear aisles and the convention improves boundary recognition enough to justify its visible pause.
